summary.text: Coastal geography studies the ever-changing zone between ocean and land, covering both its physical processes and the people who live along it.
Waves of differing strength are the main shapers of the coast: strong winter waves carry sand off beaches, while weak summer waves pile it back up.
Because waves usually hit the shore at an angle, they shift sand along the beach in one direction, a process called longshore drift that builds spits and barrier islands.

facts.label: Sea level 18,000 years ago
facts.value: Quite low, during the Pleistocene ice age

items.prompt: A beach that was wide and sandy in late summer looks much narrower after a stormy winter. Where did much of its sand go?

options.label: Blown inland to the town by winter winds
Dissolved into the cold seawater
Carried out to bars under the sea
Buried deep under the beach by rain

items.explain: Strong, destructive waves are typical of winter and shrink the beach by carrying sediment out to underwater bars.

items.prompt: A dam stops a river that used to feed sand to a coast. What can happen to beaches farther along that shore?

options.label: They grow wider as waves calm down
They stay the same, as sand never moves
They fill with mud from the dam
They can end up bare of sediment

items.explain: Longshore drift relies on a steady supply of river sediment; if that supply stops, beaches further along the shore can become bare.

items.prompt: Wind keeps throwing sea spray onto a seaside cliff, where it soaks into tiny cracks and dries. How does this wear the rock down?

options.label: Salt crystals grow in the cracks and push them apart
The water freezes each night and melts by day
Salt makes the rock soft enough to dissolve
The spray carries sand that scratches the surface

items.explain: Salt-crystal growth is the main physical weathering on beaches: the water evaporates, salt crystallises in pores and cracks, and the pressure breaks the rock.

items.prompt: Along a coast of rocky headlands and sandy bays, why do the headlands tend to wear away faster than the bays?

options.label: Headland rock is always softer than bay rock
Sand is swept off headlands but gathers in bays
Tides rise higher on headlands than in bays
Bays get more rain, which hardens their rock

items.explain: Drift carries sediment away from exposed headlands, leaving them unprotected, while sediment builds up in bays where waves are weaker and shields them from erosion.

items.prompt: About 18,000 years ago, during an ice age, sea levels were much lower than today. Why?

options.label: More of Earth's water was stored as glacier ice
The oceans' floors had sunk much deeper then
Heavy rain had not yet filled the oceans
Most seawater had evaporated into the air

items.explain: In cold periods more of Earth's water is locked up as ice in glaciers, so sea level falls; in warm periods it is released and the sea rises.

items.prompt: Rivers are the main source of beach sediment, yet long stretches of coast far from any river are covered in sand. What explains this?

options.label: Each sandy beach sits on a hidden underground river
The sand is made fresh by waves on each beach
Ships dump sand along the coast for tourists
Waves keep moving sand along the coast over time

items.explain: Longshore drift pushes sediment a little further along the beach with each wave, which is why long strips of coast are sandy, not just areas near river mouths.
